world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: naxi1246 is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping code (ISO nbf, split into nxq Naxi = naxi1245 and nru Narua = yong1270); not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title listed one title, Michaud & Vaissière 2007 ICPhS (reduplication, lexical tones and prosody in Na/Naxi). Both it and its French expanded version (Faits de langues 29, 2007) were downloaded open-access from HAL and read; saved with under Both are about lexical tone and intonational boundary-marking in reduplicated forms and are silent on word stress (word-level F0 declination + final fall; no intensity difference between reduplicated copies; 'accent' only in the keyword list). The explicit first-hand no-stress statement for Naxi is Michaud, Vaissière & Nguyen 2015 ICPhS sec. 1.1 ('no oppositions.. such . distinctive stress'), already held by the project from the naxi1245 search and re-verified here. Nothing left to acquire for this code; defer to the daughter codes. for the session was exhausted, so location was done via the HAL API only.

new_statements.quote: Naxi appears to be what is called a syllable-timed language. As such, Naxi word stress is fairly basic. Within a polysyllabic word the stress seems to be equally weighted not lending itself to a primary-secondary stress contrast. This is different than Mandarin Chinese which has words with primary stress, giving rise to neutral syllables. Naxi doesn’t appear to have neutral syllables. Our study of stress has been limited and needs further investigation.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (HAL halshs-02105442, 29 pdf pages incl. HAL cover; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Naxi phonology: a flat phonemic statement of the Longquan dialect', author Thomas M. Pinson, SIL, February 1997, CC BY-NC-SA). extracted text (printed page number 27, footer '10/25/2005 27') gives section '5. Stress and Intonation' whose first paragraph reads exactly: 'Naxi appears to be what is called a syllable-timed language. As such, Naxi word stress is fairly basic. Within a polysyllabic word the stress seems to be equally weighted not lending itself to a primary-secondary stress contrast. This is different than Mandarin Chinese which has words with primary stress, giving rise to neutral syll…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Naxi is a level-tone language (tones 55, 33, 11/21, marginal 13) with one lexical tone per syllable; there is no word-stress rule because polysyllabic words show no prominence asymmetry: all syllables are equally weighted, with no primary/secondary stress contrast and no reduced ('neutral') syllables. Corroborated first-hand by Michaud, Vaissiere & Nguyen 2015 (ICPhS, sec. 1.1, held under naxi1245): Naxi has no 'distinctive stress', and by Michaud 2003 (MSL): 'le naxi, langue sans accent lexical'. Prominence in Naxi is intonational (emphatic stress, emphatic Rising tone on L-tone syllables) and phrasal (F0 down-drift over the word/utterance, weaker grammatical morphemes).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: Pinson explicitly says the stress does not lend itself to a primary-secondary contrast.
new_statements.exceptions: Pinson: 'Our study of stress has been limited and needs further investigation'; Chinese loans bring the rising tone 13. Michaud: emphatic stress and an emphatic Rising tone exist as intonational (phrase-level) devices; grammatical morphemes are prosodically weaker and undergo syllable reduction/tone reassociation (Michaud & He 2007; He & Liu 2021).
new_statements.domain_note: Polysyllabic words of the Longquan (Baisha township) sub-dialect of Western/Lijiang Naxi, spoken forms collected 1995-97; utterance-level intonation described separately (flat to slight down-drift, also in questions). Michaud's corroboration is for the Wenhua village (Jinshan township) variety near Lijiang, also Western Naxi.
new_statements.identity_note: naxi1246 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO code nbf (split 2011 into nxq Naxi = naxi1245 and nru Narua/Yongning Na = yong1270; confirmed on the saved Glottolog page). The deciding source describes the Longquan sub-dialect (Baisha township, ~10 km N of Lijiang) of Western/Lijiang Naxi, i.e. naxi1245 [nxq]; the corroborating Michaud sources describe Wenhua village (Jinshan township, Lijiang), also naxi1245. Nothing here bears on Narua (yong1270), whose ownThe catalog record should be filed under naxi1245, not under the retired code.

new_statements.quote: Tones are lexically attached to syllables and there are extremely few processes of tonal change [20]. Phonetically, the tones are readily identifiable; there are no oppositions in the language that could complicate their production and perception, such as vowel quantity [24], phonation types, distinctive stress, or glottalized consonants [6]. Syllable structure is (C)(G)V+Tone.
new_statements.citation: Michaud, Alexis, Jacqueline Vaissière & Minh-Chau Nguyen (2015). Phonetic insights into a simple level-tone system: 'careful' vs. 'impatient' realizations of Naxi High, Mid and Low tones. Proceedings of ICPhS XVIII, Glasgow. HAL halshs-01148765,https://shs.hal.science/halshs-01148765/document
new_statements.locator: sec. 1.1, first page of the paper
new_statements.reading: Naxi (Lijiang/Western Naxi, the first author's own fieldwork variety) has no distinctive word stress; word prosody is one lexical level tone per syllable (H, M, L, marginal rising), with intonational boundary-marking (word-level F0 declination and final fall) on top. The only search-listed item for naxi1246, Michaud & Vaissière 2007 (both the ICPhS and Faits de langues versions, downloaded and read), is consistent with this but itself silent on stress: it treats Naxi as a one-tone-per-syllable language and finds no intensity prominence between reduplicated copies. The retired code naxi1246 is a bookkeeping entry; any coding should sit on the daughter codes naxi1245 (Naxi) and yong1270 (Narua).

sources.quote: En naxi, le marquage de ces frontières se réalise par une descente progressive au cours du constituant concerné, et une descente plus forte tout à la fin du constituant (Michaud 2005:41-84). ... la décroissance d'intensité de A1 à A2 et de B1 à B2 n'est que de l'ordre d'un décibel, et s'explique aisément par la différence de hauteur. [In Naxi, boundary marking is realised by a gradual descent over the constituent and a stronger descent at its very end ... the intensity decrease from A1 to A2 and B1 to B2 is only about one decibel and is easily explained by the pitch difference.]
sources.locator: postprint pp. 27-28 (sec. on diachronic hypothesis) and results section (intensity/open quotient)
sources.note: Silent on word stress; same content as the ICPhS paper. Word-boundary marking is F0 declination plus final fall; intensity and open-quotient differences between reduplicated copies are negligible/non-significant. No claim of a stressed syllable in Naxi words.

sources.citation: Michaud, Alexis & Jacqueline Vaissière (2007). The phonetic evolution of reduplicated expressions: reduplication, lexical tones and prosody in Na (Naxi). Proceedings of the 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS XVI), Saarbrücken, pp. 801-804. HAL halshs-00166896.
sources.quote: In Na, there is a downtrend within each constituent: a gentle decrease in F0 in the course of the constituent at issue (e.g. in the course of the phonological word), followed by a faster and stronger downward tilt in F0 at the end of the constituent [4:41-84]. ... No significant difference in RMS amplitude was found between A1 and A2 or B1 and B2.
sources.note: Silent on word stress. First-hand fieldwork on Lijiang Naxi and Fengke Naxi; the paper is about lexical tone (H/M/L + rare LH, one tone per syllable) and the tonal outcome of reduplication (H>HM, L>ML, M>MM; ABAB unchanged), explained as phonologised intonational boundary-marking (word-level F0 declination + final fall). No intensity difference between the two copies in ABAB reduplicated forms (no positional prominence). 'Accent' appears only in the keyword list, never applied to Naxi in the body. Hypothesises an earlier word-tone (not word-stress) stage after Mazaudon p.c.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences

sources.note: The paper is about segmental sound changes (palatalization of velars, vowels /i/ /y/ /o/) inferred from Bonin's 1903 French-orthography word list; it never states the Naxi stress or tone system. The only tone statement is that Bonin's list marks no tones. Present-day Lijiang Naxi forms are given with tone letters (e.g. ʐwɑ˧ 'horse', ku˧ly˧ 'head', /ŋɤ˩/, /æ˩/, /nɑ˩˥/ 'you', /lɑ˩/ 'hand', [tʰø˧pv̩˥] 'fabric', /kɯ˧ʈʂɯ˩/), which presuppose a tonal system with mid, low, high and rising categories, but no inventory or rule is stated. Nothing on stress, weight, domain or secondary stress.

sources.citation: Michaud, Alexis (2006). Tonal reassociation and rising tonal contours in Naxi. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 29. pp. 61-94.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Western Naxi has three tones (High, Mid and Low) plus a more recent rising contour tone. [...] Naxi appears as a textbook example of level-tone language: each syllable carries a High ( ́), Mid ( ̄), or Low ( ̀) lexical tone (hereafter H, M, L). However, a rising tone is also reported on a small set of 'native' words as well as on numerous loanwords.
sources.note: Tone system: three level lexical tones H, M, L on every syllable, plus a marginal rising contour /LH/ (and /MH/) arising from (i) reduction of an enclitic H-tone morpheme (/tɑ́/ 'only', /pú/ 'to bring', /nɯ́/ 'or') whose floating H reassociates leftward onto a preceding L- or M-tone syllable (p. 64-65), (ii) optional 'intensive' H-tone addition on L/M syllables (section 2.1), (iii) a no-longer-productive possessive H-tone construction on 'native' rising-tone words (Part II), (iv) syllabic coalescence (p. 85), and (v) Chinese loanwords, 15% of ~1,000 basic Chinese words elicited in AS carry /LH
